q: Ordering a Pinot Gris and expecting something dry, a guest meets a wine with obvious sweetness. What explains it?
opts: The wine had restarted its fermentation in the bottle
Pinot Gris may not legally be fermented dry in this region
Any Alsace wine above 13 percent alcohol retains sugar by law
Sweetness varies from producer to producer within one appellation
exp: House style, not law, decides where a Pinot Gris finishes, and the same appellation covers bone-dry and frankly sweet bottlings. From the 2021 vintage an Alsace white must state its sweetness on the label, as sec, demi-sec, moelleux or doux or on a printed scale, so a current bottle declares itself and only an older one has to be asked about or tasted.

q: A neutral, earthy, generously cropping white was once the workhorse of the region and now survives best in the north around Mittelbergheim. Which grape?
exp: Sylvaner yields more juice and less perfume than the noble four. On the right site it turns dry and saline rather than dilute, and it is the regional match for onion tart and shellfish.

q: One Grand Cru site breaks the four-variety rule to admit Sylvaner, in recognition of a long local tradition. Which site?
exp: Zotzenberg at Mittelbergheim had produced serious Sylvaner on its marl and limestone for generations, and the decree was amended to let it say so. It is the only Grand Cru where that name may appear.

q: Soft, appley and low in acid, one white makes an undemanding everyday wine and much of the base for the region's sparkling. Which?
exp: It has neither Riesling's acidity nor Gewurztraminer's perfume, and that neutrality is exactly what a base wine wants. It is also a staple of the carafe list in an Alsace winstub.

q: A bottle labelled Pinot Blanc in Alsace may legally contain none of that grape at all. What is likely inside instead?
exp: The two are interplanted, blended and sold under the one name. Auxerrois is rounder and lower in acid, so a notably fat, broad Pinot Blanc is usually mostly Auxerrois.

q: A white grape of the region shares its name with the black grape that Cahors uses for its wine. Which white grape?
exp: Cahors calls Malbec Auxerrois. The Alsace Auxerrois is a white Pinot relative, born of the same Pinot and Gouais Blanc crossing that gave Chardonnay, and the two share nothing but the word.

q: Two label terms differing by a single letter, one ending in -ner and the other in -ener, point to different grapes entirely. Which reading is correct?
opts: Klevner is Gewurztraminer; Klevener de Heiligenstein is Riesling
Klevner is Pinot Blanc; Klevener de Heiligenstein is Savagnin Rose
Both are local synonyms for Pinot Blanc
Klevner is Sylvaner; Klevener de Heiligenstein is Pinot Gris
exp: Klevner is simply the Alsatian word for Pinot Blanc. Klevener de Heiligenstein is Savagnin Rose, a plainer cousin of Gewurztraminer grown in a handful of communes in the Bas-Rhin and nowhere else in France.

q: One old variety, as much a table grape as a wine grape, has shrunk to about one percent of the region's plantings and what is left disappears into Edelzwicker. Which?
exp: Chasselas is as much a table grape as a wine grape, early and neutral. What is left of it disappears into Edelzwicker, and it is Switzerland rather than Alsace that takes it seriously.

q: Schlossberg was the first site raised to the region's top tier, a generation after most of France had settled its appellations. In which year?
exp: The first decree came in 1975 and named Schlossberg alone. Decrees in 1983 and 1992 took the list to fifty, and Kaefferkopf was added in 2007 to make fifty-one, which leaves this among the youngest classifications in France.

q: Named Grand Cru sites in the region now come to which figure?
exp: Each is separately delimited, with its own boundaries, permitted varieties and maximum crop. The great majority lie in the southern half of the region, in the Haut-Rhin.

q: Four varieties alone may normally be bottled at Grand Cru level. Which set?
opts: Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Auxerrois and Sylvaner
Riesling, Sylvaner, Pinot Blanc and Pinot Noir
Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Blanc and Chardonnay
Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris and Muscat
exp: These are the four noble grapes, and outside a handful of named exceptions the restriction is absolute. Where a single variety is used it is named on the label beside the site, though the sites cleared for a blend name no grape at all. Since the 2022 vintage Pinot Noir may also be bottled as a red at Hengst, Kirchberg de Barr and Vorbourg.

q: Reading an Alsace Grand Cru label beside a Burgundy Grand Cru label, one difference is immediately visible. What is it?
opts: The Alsace label states the yield in hectolitres per hectare
The Alsace label names a grape variety alongside the vineyard
The Alsace label leaves out the vintage
The Alsace label gives the commune in place of the vineyard
exp: Varietal labelling is the regional norm and it carries straight into the top tier. Burgundy names the climat and expects you to know the grape from the colour of the wine.

q: Rules at Grand Cru level are tighter than for the regional appellation above all in which respect?
opts: A compulsory period of ageing in new oak barrels
A lower maximum yield and a higher minimum ripeness
A ban on stating the vintage anywhere on the label
A requirement to blend at least three permitted varieties
exp: The decree cuts the permitted crop sharply, raises the minimum must weight and requires the fruit to be picked by hand. Nothing in it says anything about oak.

q: One statement is compulsory on every Grand Cru label that is optional further down the hierarchy. Which?
opts: The yield in hectolitres per hectare
exp: A Grand Cru must come from a single year and must declare it, alongside the site and the variety. Ordinary Alsace may be blended across vintages and sold without a year.

q: The steepest of the Grands Crus, and the southernmost, rises above Thann on dark volcanic rock. Which is it?
exp: Rangen is the only Grand Cru on volcanic soil, and its slope is severe enough that growers carry washed-out soil back up the hill after storms. The wines are smoky and austere in youth.

q: Two Grands Crus depart from the single-variety rule and permit a blend of grapes in one wine. Which pair?
exp: Both sites have a long history of co-planted field blends, so their decrees preserve the practice. Everywhere else in the tier the wine must be a single named variety.
